title: Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing
hookLine: the All-Knowing, who knows the hidden and the seen
tomorrow: a heavy, tight week. is it a punishment, or something else?

cards: Phones have a hidden folder, a locked note, a version never sent. Yesterday ended on Amira's worry, the one she hasn't told anyone. Who already knows?
The Qur'an's answer sits in a verse with a strange detail in it. In Pickthall's words: "Not a leaf falleth but He knoweth it." Of everything in the universe to mention, why a single falling leaf?

teach.b: Read the whole verse and the leaf starts to make sense. It opens as big as it can: "And with Him are the keys of the Invisible. None but He knoweth them."

teach.h: LAND, SEA, A LEAF, A GRAIN.
teach.b: Then it comes down to the world you can see: the land and the sea. Then smaller: a leaf, falling. Then smaller and darker: a grain, buried in the earth where no one could ever look.
Then everything wet or dry, all of it kept in a clear record.

teach.h: A ZOOM, DOWN TO THE SMALLEST.
teach.b: The verse is a zoom, from the keys of the unseen down to one seed in the dark. That's the solve. A leaf is the thing nobody watches fall.
Not the gardener, not the kid under the tree. If the verse names that, then nothing is too small or too hidden to be known.
That's today's name, al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, who knows the hidden and the seen. For some people that's a frightening thought. Read slowly, it can also be a comfort.
A worry you haven't put into words for anyone is not a secret from Him. You don't have to explain it from the beginning. It was known before you found the words.
Here's one for a friend tonight: in this verse, a grain in the dark earth gets the same attention as the keys of the unseen.

how: Muslims bring private worries to Allah in du'a, in any language and in silence if they wish, trusting that al-'Alim already knows what is in the heart.

o: the One who sees only the deeds people do
the One who teaches people all they know
the One who knows the hidden and the seen

games.q: the verse that zooms in — tap the pairs.
p: a grain in the dark earth
knows the hidden and the seen

s: al-'Alim knowing everything is meant only as a warning
it can also be a comfort: an untold worry isn't a secret from Him.
the verse moves from the keys of the unseen down to a single grain
keys, land and sea, a leaf, a grain in the dark, everything wet or dry.
a du'a has to be said out loud in Arabic to count
a silent worry in plain words is known to al-'Alim; he knows what hasn't been said.

games.q: a friend asks: 'why does that verse bother mentioning one falling leaf?' what's the solve?
o: it zooms down to the smallest unwatched thing: nothing is too small to be known.
the leaf is a symbol for death, so the verse is a warning about dying.
leaves were sacred in Arabia, so the verse is honoring trees.
games.why: the verse runs from the keys of the Invisible down to a grain in the dark. the leaf is the thing nobody watches fall, and it's known.

practice: Close your eyes and let one worry you haven't told anyone come up, without saying it aloud.

If you pray, you can tell it to Him silently, in your own plain words, as a believer would to al-'Alim; if not, just name it to yourself, clearly, once. Then sit with it known, and let the breath carry on.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Alim: the All-Knowing, who knows the hidden and the seen, down to a leaf falling where no one is watching.

carryVoice: Keep this one near: he knows, even the leaf nobody saw fall. See you tomorrow.
